beats.intro: Chapter seven, lesson five. Facilitated diffusion and active transport. [[door]]A plain gate lets anyone walk through. A revolving door makes you wait your turn, and works in a rhythm. [[cells]]A cell membrane has both kinds of crossing, and more. [[patch]]Here is our patch of membrane again. [[lit]]Today we light up the transport proteins: the channels, the carriers, and the pumps.
beats.facil: Last time, only small nonpolar molecules slipped through the bilayer easily. Ions, water, and sugars need help. [[fd]]That help is called facilitated diffusion. Transport proteins speed up the passive movement of molecules across the membrane. Passive, so it takes no energy, and it still runs down the concentration gradient, from crowded to sparse. [[channel]]A channel protein is a corridor. It lets one specific molecule or ion cross. [[aqua]]Aquaporins are channels for water. [[gated]]Gated ion channels open or close in response to a stimulus, such as a chemical signal or a change in voltage. So the cell decides when the ions flow. [[carrier]]A carrier protein works differently. It binds the solute, then undergoes a subtle change in shape that moves the binding site across the membrane. Open to the outside, bind, change shape, open to the inside, release. Just like a revolving door. [[down]]Either way, the solute travels down its gradient, so no energy is needed.
beats.q1: Quick check. Is each one a channel, or a carrier?
beats.active: [[problem]]But sometimes a cell needs the opposite. It needs sodium out, even though sodium is already crowded outside. [[against]]Active transport moves a solute against its concentration gradient, from sparse to crowded. That takes energy, usually from {{ATP|A T P}}. [[atp]]Think of rolling a ball uphill. The ball will not climb by itself, so the cell pays in {{ATP|A T P}}. [[protein]]It is done by specific proteins embedded in the membrane, and it lets cells keep concentrations that differ from their surroundings. [[note]]So remember the difference. Channels and carriers can only let things run downhill. A pump can push them uphill.
beats.pump: The best known example is the sodium-potassium pump. Outside the cell, sodium is high and potassium is low. Inside, it is the reverse. [[s1]]Step one. The pump is open to the cytoplasm, and three sodium ions bind. [[s2]]Step two. {{ATP|A T P}} gives a phosphate to the pump, and becomes {{ADP|A D P}}. The pump changes shape. [[s3]]Step three. Now it opens to the outside, and releases the three sodium ions into the extracellular fluid. [[s4]]Step four. Two potassium ions bind from the outside, and the phosphate comes off. [[s5]]Step five. Without the phosphate, the pump returns to its first shape, open to the cytoplasm, holding the potassium. [[s6]]Step six. It releases the two potassium ions into the cytoplasm, and the cycle starts again. [[count]]Each turn costs one {{ATP|A T P}}, sends three sodium ions out, and brings two potassium ions in.
beats.q2: Quick check. What does each turn of the pump move?
beats.example: Let's put channels and pumps together. [[chan]]A gated sodium channel opens. Sodium is crowded outside, so it flows in, downhill, with no energy. [[fill]]If nothing else happened, sodium would keep building up inside the cell. [[pump]]So the sodium-potassium pump pushes it back out, uphill, paying {{ATP|A T P}}. [[bal]]The channel lets it in. The pump sends it out. That is how a cell keeps its sodium low inside.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[diff]]Plain diffusion needs no protein and no energy, and runs downhill. [[fac]]Facilitated diffusion uses a channel or a carrier, and is still downhill and passive. Both of these are passive transport. [[act]]Active transport uses a pump and {{ATP|A T P}} to go uphill, as the sodium-potassium pump does, three sodium out, two potassium in. [[end]]Now try the practice.
